#| label: original-study

# Wang et al. (2026), section 3.2, Experiment 1 (N = 123).
# Outcome is NS+: category paired with a rewarded originally CHOSEN item.
# Unchosen-item inference predicts OR < 1; do not reverse this label.
# Published central estimates and 95% HPD intervals are entered without
# reconstructing individual-level data from rounded odds ratios.
original_n <- 123L
original <- tibble(
  pair_type = c("chosen", "unchosen"),
  odds_ratio = c(2.01, 0.69),
  lower = c(1.46, 0.52), upper = c(2.79, 0.91), N = original_n
)
original_trial_type_or <- c(estimate = 0.44, lower = 0.36, upper = 0.55)
# Aggregate-only reproduction of original Rmd preprocessing/power calculation.
# The source Rmd's section "Power analysis for Exp 2" operates on Exp1 data.
original_summary <- fromJSON("original-exp1-summary.json")
stopifnot(original_summary$reproduced_model_n == 123L,
          original_summary$reproduced_model_trials == 5892L)
original_d <- abs(original_summary$unchosen_cohens_d)

# Key statistics


```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr list(ids = c(experiment_id, experiment_id_phase2), hashes = tools::md5sum(analysis_input_files[file.exists(analysis_input_files)]), rstanarm = as.character(packageVersion("rstanarm")))
# Source: OSF xjhkf, Experiment_1_analysis.Rmd, revised main model
# ("Edit of the main model by Xinyue") and separate chosen/unchosen models.
# Source-code preprocessing, including 300 < rating RT < 8000 ms, category
# means rounded to 2 decimals, and absolute separately z-scored left/right
# means, is reproduced. This differs from the paper's signed-difference prose.
as_bool <- function(x) tolower(as.character(x)) %in% "true"
score_attention_checks <- function(trials) {
  attention <- trials |> filter(task == "attention_check")
  if (!nrow(attention)) return(tibble(
    participant_id = character(), n_attention_checks = integer(),
    n_attention_correct = integer(), n_attention_nonresponses = integer(),
    attention_accuracy = double(), attention_nonresponse_rate = double()))
  attention |>
    mutate(attention_nonresponse = is.na(response) | response == "" |
             tolower(response) == "null",
           attention_correct = !attention_nonresponse & !is.na(letter) &
             tolower(response) == tolower(letter)) |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(n_attention_checks = n(),
              n_attention_correct = sum(attention_correct),
              n_attention_nonresponses = sum(attention_nonresponse), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(attention_accuracy = n_attention_correct / n_attention_checks,
           attention_nonresponse_rate = n_attention_nonresponses / n_attention_checks)
}
read_phase <- function(id) {
  dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id)
  if (!all(file.exists(file.path(dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))) return(NULL)
  read_export <- function(name) read_csv(file.path(dir, name),
    col_types = cols(.default = col_character()), show_col_types = FALSE)
  participants <- read_export("participants.csv") |>
    mutate(completed = as_bool(completed), practice_misses = as.numeric(practice_misses))
  trials <- read_export("trials.csv")
  errors <- if (file.exists(file.path(dir, "errors.csv"))) read_export("errors.csv") else tibble()
  # Descriptive attention scores use all presented checks as the denominator.
  # Missing responses count as incorrect.
  attention <- score_attention_checks(trials)
  participants <- participants |> left_join(attention, by = "participant_id") |>
    mutate(across(c(n_attention_checks, n_attention_correct, n_attention_nonresponses),
                  ~ coalesce(.x, 0L)))
  complete <- participants |> filter(completed)
  # Completed export flag replaces the original platform's nonempty unique_code.
  # As in the original, a missed repeated practice choice ends the session, so
  # completion carries the practice exclusion; answered repeats do not exclude.
  # No memory-accuracy cutoff is added.
  keep <- complete |> filter(!as_bool(qa_run), !as_bool(preview_run))
  retained <- trials |> filter(participant_id %in% keep$participant_id)
  ratings <- retained |> filter(task == "preference_rating") |>
    mutate(rt = as.numeric(rt), rating = as.numeric(rating)) |>
    filter(rt > 300, rt < 8000) |>
    group_by(participant_id, category) |>
    summarise(mean_rating = round(mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE), 2), .groups = "drop")
  choices <- retained |> filter(task == "final_choice") |>
    mutate(rt = as.numeric(rt), timed_out = as_bool(timed_out),
      p_ns = if_else(timed_out, NA_integer_, as.integer(as_bool(chose_paired_reward))),
      chosen_trial_centered = as.integer(pair_type == "unchosen")) |>
    left_join(ratings |> rename(Left_mean_ratings = mean_rating),
      by = c("participant_id", "left_category" = "category")) |>
    left_join(ratings |> rename(Right_mean_ratings = mean_rating),
      by = c("participant_id", "right_category" = "category")) |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    mutate(z_score_norm_drate_by_outcome = abs(as.numeric(scale(Left_mean_ratings)) -
                                               as.numeric(scale(Right_mean_ratings)))) |>
    ungroup()
  # A missed choice is missing, never silently interpreted as a right choice.
  # Missing final-choice responses are excluded consistently across exports.
  model_data <- choices |> filter(!is.na(p_ns), is.finite(z_score_norm_drate_by_outcome)) |>
    mutate(pid = factor(participant_id))
  list(participants = participants, trials = trials, errors = errors, attention = attention,
    complete = complete, keep = keep, retained = retained, choices = choices,
    model_data = model_data,
    n_no_response = sum(vapply(split(choices$timed_out, choices$participant_id), all, logical(1))))
}

fit_source_model <- function(data, formula) {
  # Original analysis: normal(0,2.5), decov(regularization=1), seed123,
  # four chains, 4000 iterations, first2000 warmup, random participant intercept.
  fit <- rstanarm::stan_glmer(formula = formula, data = data,
    family = binomial(link = "logit"),
    prior = rstanarm::normal(0, 2.5),
    prior_intercept = rstanarm::normal(0, 2.5),
    prior_covariance = rstanarm::decov(regularization = 1),
    chains = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 123, refresh = 0)
  sampler <- rstan::get_sampler_params(fit$stanfit, inc_warmup = FALSE)
  divergent <- sum(vapply(sampler, function(s) sum(s[, "divergent__"]), numeric(1)))
  if (divergent > 0) {
    # Diagnostic-only sampler adjustment; formula/priors/chains/iterations unchanged.
    # The first source-default pilot fit had2 divergences in the chosen-only model.
    fit <- update(fit, adapt_delta = 0.99, refresh = 0)
    attr(fit, "tolerance_tightened") <- TRUE
  }
  fit
}
fit_phase <- function(d) {
  if (is.null(d) || n_distinct(d$model_data$pid) < 2) return(NULL)
  x <- d$model_data
  if (!all(c("chosen", "unchosen") %in% x$pair_type)) return(NULL)
  fits <- list(
    main = fit_source_model(x,
      p_ns ~ chosen_trial_centered * z_score_norm_drate_by_outcome + (1 | pid)),
    chosen = fit_source_model(filter(x, pair_type == "chosen"),
      p_ns ~ z_score_norm_drate_by_outcome + (1 | pid)),
    unchosen = fit_source_model(filter(x, pair_type == "unchosen"),
      p_ns ~ z_score_norm_drate_by_outcome + (1 | pid)))
  attr(fits, "N") <- n_distinct(x$pid)
  fits
}
or_summary <- function(fit, term = "(Intercept)") {
  draws <- as.matrix(fit)[, term]
  hpdi <- coda::HPDinterval(coda::mcmc(draws), prob = 0.95)[1, ]
  tibble(odds_ratio = exp(median(draws)), lower = exp(hpdi[1]), upper = exp(hpdi[2]),
    posterior_probability_below_one = mean(draws < 0))
}
model_summary <- function(fits) {
  if (is.null(fits)) return(tibble())
  bind_rows(or_summary(fits$chosen) |> mutate(pair_type = "chosen"),
            or_summary(fits$unchosen) |> mutate(pair_type = "unchosen")) |>
    mutate(N = attr(fits, "N"))
}
diagnostics <- function(fits) {
  if (is.null(fits)) return(tibble())
  imap_dfr(fits, function(fit, name) {
    summary <- summary(fit, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
    sampler <- rstan::get_sampler_params(fit$stanfit, inc_warmup = FALSE)
    tibble(Model = name, `Maximum Rhat` = max(summary[, "Rhat"], na.rm = TRUE),
      `Minimum effective N` = min(summary[, "n_eff"], na.rm = TRUE),
      Divergences = sum(vapply(sampler, function(s) sum(s[, "divergent__"]), numeric(1))),
      `Sampler tolerance tightened` = isTRUE(attr(fit, "tolerance_tightened")))
  })
}
# Forest plot matching the presentation's results slide: unchosen (primary) above
# chosen, one row per study, original in grey, labels "OR [HPDI]" on the right.
comparison_plot <- function(..., pair = c("unchosen", "chosen")) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || nrow(.x) == 0)]
  palette <- setNames(c("#9AA3B2", "#1F6FB5", "#2A9D8F")[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))
  all_rows <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y))
  # Axis limits from every row, so separate unchosen and chosen figures share one axis.
  x_limits <- range(c(0.45, 3.2, all_rows$lower, all_rows$upper), na.rm = TRUE)
  plotted <- all_rows |> filter(pair_type %in% pair) |>
    mutate(Row = paste0(Study, " (N = ", N, ")"),
      Panel = factor(if_else(pair_type == "unchosen", "Unchosen\n(primary)", "Chosen"),
                     levels = c("Unchosen\n(primary)", "Chosen")),
      Label = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", odds_ratio, lower, upper))
  plotted$Row <- factor(plotted$Row, levels = rev(unique(plotted$Row[order(match(plotted$Study, names(studies)))])))
  facets <- if (length(pair) > 1)
    facet_grid(Panel ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", switch = "y") else NULL
  ggplot(plotted, aes(x = odds_ratio, y = Row, colour = Study)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), width = 0.25, linewidth = 0.9, orientation = "y") +
    geom_point(size = 3.2) +
    geom_text(aes(x = Inf, label = Label), hjust = -0.08, size = 3.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 1, 2, 3), labels = c("0.5", "1", "2", "3"), limits = x_limits) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = palette, guide = "none") +
    facets +
    coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
    labs(x = "Odds ratio for choosing NS+ (log scale): < 1 avoid, > 1 prefer", y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(strip.placement = "outside",
          strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, face = "bold", hjust = 1),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
          plot.margin = margin(5.5, 125, 5.5, 5.5))
}
phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2)
have_data <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
phase1_fits <- fit_phase(phase1)
phase2_fits <- fit_phase(phase2)
phase1_estimates <- model_summary(phase1_fits)
phase2_estimates <- model_summary(phase2_fits)
format_hpdi <- function(lower, upper) ifelse(is.na(lower) | is.na(upper), "Not available",
  paste0("[", formatC(lower, format = "g", digits = 3), ", ", formatC(upper, format = "g", digits = 3), "]"))
```

# The summary, addendum, and Results share the same excluded Phase 1 data.
key_phase1_data <- phase1
key_phase1_n <- if (is.null(phase1)) NA_integer_ else n_distinct(phase1$model_data$pid)
key_phase1_estimates <- phase1_estimates

key_row <- function(study, estimates, n, collected) {
  if (!collected) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "not yet collected", OR = "not yet collected", `95% HPDI` = ""))
  }
  if (!nrow(estimates)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(n), OR = "not estimable", `95% HPDI` = ""))
  }
  estimates |> filter(pair_type == "unchosen") |>
    transmute(Study = study, N = as.character(N),
              OR = formatC(odds_ratio, format = "f", digits = 3),
              `95% HPDI` = format_hpdi(lower, upper))
}
key_rows <- bind_rows(
  key_row("Original", original, original_n, TRUE),
  key_row("Phase 1: replication", key_phase1_estimates, key_phase1_n, !is.null(key_phase1_data)),
  key_row("Phase 2: extension", phase2_estimates,
          if (is.null(phase2)) NA_integer_ else n_distinct(phase2$model_data$pid), !is.null(phase2))
)
key_rows |> knitr::kable(caption = "Unchosen-category model intercept: odds of choosing the category paired with a rewarded chosen item. OR below1 indicates the predicted inverse preference. Original: Wang et al. (2026), section3.2; Phase 1: posterior median OR and exponentiated log-odds HPDI.")

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction

I’m interested in how memory and decision-making interact to support adaptive behavior, including how information from past experiences can guide decisions in novel situations. Wang et al. (2026) found that value inferred for an unchosen option generalized to novel objects within the same semantic category. I would like to specifically replicate the finding that participants preferred novel items that were semantically similar to an unchosen option whose chosen counterpart received no reward over novel items related to an unchosen option whose chosen counterpart was rewarded, because it suggested how we generalize value beyond direct experience to make adaptive decisions.

The original study reported using 128 object images, with 16 from each of eight semantic categories in the DinoLab Object Database. Participants were asked to repeatedly choose one item from each pair that they predicted would be more valuable and justify their decisions during deliberation phase. They then learned whether the chosen items received a reward or no reward during outcome learning phase. In the final decision phase, they chose between novel exemplars from all categories to test whether previously learned and inferred value of unchosen options generalized to novel objects from the same semantic categories. A surprise memory test of item and associative memory was conducted to understand the relationship between memory for original associations and novel decisions.

The key statistical test was a multilevel Bayesian logistic regression testing whether participants’ selection of novel items depended on whether the corresponding previously seen unchosen item had been paired with a chosen item that received a reward or no reward.

## Methods

### Power analysis

```{r}
#| label: power
# Source Exp1 Rmd lines925-946: one-sample, two-sided t-test against0.5
# on participant-level unchosen NS+ proportions; Cohen d=t/sqrt(N).
# This is the authors' planning approximation, NOT power for stan_glmer.
# Basis is original data only, never the three-person pilot effect.
power_rows <- map_dfr(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95), function(pw) {
  out <- pwr::pwr.t.test(d = original_d, sig.level = 0.05, power = pw,
                       type = "one.sample", alternative = "two.sided")
  tibble(Power = scales::percent(pw), `Required participants` = ceiling(out$n))
})
power_rows |> knitr::kable(caption = sprintf(
  "Original-code planning approximation: one-sample two-sided t-test, alpha=.05, absolute Cohen d=%.4f, based on original Exp1 unchosen proportions (N=%d). Not a direct power calculation for the Bayesian hierarchical model.",
  original_d, original_summary$unchosen_subject_n))
# Compatibility for the template's inline expressions; student must replace
# its obsolete gain/loss prose. This within-person design has ONE sample N.
two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * original_n)
```

For comparison, 2.5 times the original sample would be 308 (rounded up from 307.5) usable participants in total.

### Planned sample

The experiment will recruit U.S. residents aged 18-35 who are fluent in English through Prolific. Participants must complete the experiment on a computer with a keyboard. Participants who fail to respond to both the initial and repeated presentation of a timed practice choice, or who do not complete the experiment, will be excluded. Data collection will continue until 118 participants pass the exclusion criteria, providing approximately 80% power.

### Materials

Wang et al. (2026) described the stimuli as follows:

> “The image stimuli were taken from the DinoLab Object Database” (p. 2, §2.2).

> “128 images of common objects from 8 semantic categories (16 objects per category): land mammals, ocean creatures, vegetables, fruits, sports, vehicles, musical instruments, and buildings.” (p. 2, §2.2).

The original Experiment 1 data, however, contain 15 fruit images, 17 sports images, and 16 images in each of the other six categories, for a total of 128 images. The replication uses the same stimuli from the DinoLab Object Database, with one exception: an image of a cinnamon bun that was incorrectly categorized as an ocean creature was removed. The replication stimuli set has 15 fruit images, 15 ocean creatures images, 17 sports images and 16 images in each of the other five categories, for a total of 127 images. Although the resulting differences in category pool sizes slightly affect the probability of each image being randomly selected, each category still contributes the same number of images to the design. No new images were added, so all stimuli used in the replication were what participants saw in the original experiment.

[Stimulus files](https://github.com/psych251/wang2026/tree/main/stimuli)

### Procedure

1.  Consent and introduction: Participants provide Stanford course consent and receive instructions to build a valuable stamp portfolio by selecting pictures. Adaptation: Course consent and reconstructed instructions based on original instructions for better clarity.

2.  Pre-experimental phase: Participants rate 24 randomized pictures (three from each of eight categories) “based on their personal preferences” using a slide bar on a 0-100 scale.

3.  Deliberation phase: Participants “choose the images they predicted would be placed on the most valuable stamp” across four pairs repeated in two practice rounds and one final round (12 choices in total). Participants press J to choose the left option and K to choose the right option. Practice choices are timed (5s), while final choices are untimed. The second practice round requires written justifications for their choices.

4.  Choice Outcome phase: Four chosen pictures receive randomly assigned outcomes (two rewarded, two unrewarded), with pictures shown alone for 1 s followed by “reward or no reward” for 2 s with pictures. Unchosen pictures receive no feedback.

5.  Final Decision phase: Participants make 48 timed (7s) choices (24 chosen-category and 24 unchosen-category pairs) using six new pictures per category, each presented twice. Participants need to press keys shown on the screen to pass occasional attention checks.

6.  Surprise Memory phase: Participants respond to eight old/new recognition trials (four chosen and four unseen pictures; 1 = old, 0 = new). When an original picture is correctly recognized, participants need to choose its paired partner from four options.

7.  Optional final questions: Participants answer demographic, instruction-clarity, and feedback questions. Adaptation: Course-template questions.

8.  Debrief and completion: Participants learn the study purpose and that outcomes were randomly assigned and complete submitting their responses. Adaptation: Course-specific debrief.

Participants are expected to finish the entire experiment in 10-20 minutes.

### Analysis plan

**Key analysis of interest.** Participants are predicted to prefer novel items from unchosen categories whose chosen counterparts received no reward, than those whose counterparts were rewarded. It will be tested using a multilevel Bayesian logistic regression on the 24 unchosen-category decisions per participant, controlling for initial category preferences and including a random intercept for each participant. The effect size will be reported as an odds ratio with a 95% credible interval.

**Secondary confirmatory and exploratory analyses.** Secondary confirmatory analyses will use multilevel Bayesian logistic regressions for chosen-category decisions and for chosen- and unchosen-category decisions combined. Exploratory follow-up analyses may include the original study’s Bayesian multilevel analyses of RT and adaptive choice, descriptive memory summaries, and memory–choice analyses using Spearman correlations and permutation tests.

**Exclusions.** Participants are excluded if they fail to respond on both the initial and repeated presentation of any timed practice trial or do not complete the study.

### Differences from the original study

| Aspect | Original study | This replication | Expected to matter? |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Sample | University of Chicago SONA and MTurk/CloudResearch | Prolific | Unlikely. Participants will be recruited using the same eligibility criteria. |
| Exclusion | The paper reports termination after three missed practice trials, while the original code and data show a different stopping rule. | Following the original code and data, a missed practice choice triggers a 3-s warning and one repeat of the same pair. If the repeated choice is also missed, the session ends. | Unlikely. It follows the actual procedure so it should have a comparable exclusion rate to the original's. |
| Stimuli | Ocean creatures category includes a cinnamon bun. | Removed the cinnamon bun. | Unlikely. The removal ensures that all stimuli better match their intended semantic categories. |
| Paradigm | The paper reports a 5-s response window for practice trials, while the original data suggest a 7-s window. | Used the 5-s window described in the paper. | Unlikely, although the shorter window may result in more missed responses. |
| Paradigm | The code includes untimed attention checks, while the original data suggest a 15-s response window. | Added a 15-s response window for attention checks. | Unlikely. Attention-check performance is recorded for descriptive purposes and does not affect participant exclusion. |
| Paradigm | The paper describes using two lure items from different categories in the memory test while the data show two items from the same category. | Used two lure images from the same novel category, following the original data. | Unlikely. This follows the procedure reflected in the original data. |
| Instructions | Long paragraphs in the original SVG instructions. | Reconstructed shorter phase-specific instructions for better clarity and corrected typos. | Unlikely, although differences in wording could affect participants' understanding of the task. |
| Data | Missed choices were coded as selections of the right-side image. | Excluded missed choices from the choice models to reduce noise. | Unlikely. Only 30 of 5,892 trials (0.5%) were missed in the original model data. |
| Analysis | The code uses the absolute rating difference, while the paper describes a signed difference. | Used the absolute difference, consistent with the original code. | Unlikely. The published estimates were based on the absolute difference. |

### Methods addendum (post data collection)

#### Actual sample

```{r}
#| label: no-data-notice
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!have_data) {
  cat(

    "`npm run export -- --experiment ", experiment_id, " --key <path to your key>` and render again. ",
    "If you have exported, check that `experiment_id` at the top of this file matches ",
    "`EXPERIMENT.id` in `experiment.js`.\n",
    ":::\n", sep = "")
}

Of the 159 recorded sessions, 1 participant declined consent, 16 participants missed the repeated practice choice and were excluded according to the preregistered exclusion rule, and 25 participants did not complete the study. The remaining 117 participants completed the study and were retained for analysis. The median completion time was 11.6 minutes (range: 4.2–48.7 minutes).

#### Deviations from the preregistered plan

A total of 118 participants were marked as completed on Prolific, as planned. However, one participant did not provide complete data and was excluded, leaving a final sample of 117 participants. Additional post hoc analyses were conducted after inspecting the data and were not specified in the preregistration. The preregistration also noted that exploratory analyses might include descriptive memory summaries, one of which was not included in the final analyses.

## Results

### Data preparation

Following the original analysis code, ratings with response times outside the 300-8000 ms range were excluded. This resulted in the removal of 333 out of 2,808 ratings (11.9%), all of which exceeded 8000 ms. Eight participants (across 12 participant-category combinations) had no valid ratings remaining for at least one category, resulting in 130 final-choice trials without the corresponding rating covariate, which were excluded from the analyses. An additional 27 final-choice trials were excluded due to timeouts. The final models included 2,710 unchosen and 2,749 chosen trials.

### Confirmatory analysis

#### Primary analysis

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| results: asis
# The primary model matches the Introduction and Methods: unchosen trials only.
# Chosen and combined models are reported below as secondary analyses.
if (!is.null(phase1_fits)) {
  primary_fit <- phase1_fits$unchosen
  cat("```text\n")
  print(primary_fit, digits = 3)
  cat("\n```\n\n")
  primary_fixed <- rstanarm::fixef(primary_fit)
  primary_table <- map_dfr(names(primary_fixed), function(term)
    or_summary(primary_fit, term) |> mutate(Term = term)) |>
    select(Term, everything())
  cat(knitr::kable(primary_table, digits = 3,
    caption = "Primary confirmatory analysis: unchosen-category model, adjusted for the source-code rating covariate. Intercept OR below 1 is the predicted inverse preference."), sep = "\n")
  cat("\n\n")
  cat(knitr::kable(diagnostics(phase1_fits["unchosen"]), digits = 3,
    caption = "MCMC diagnostics for the primary unchosen-category model."), sep = "\n")
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

#### Secondary analyses

```{r}

                          `Combined model` = phase1_fits$main)

        else ". Adjusted for the source-code rating covariate.")), sep = "\n")
    cat("\n\n")
  }
  cat(knitr::kable(diagnostics(secondary_models), digits = 3,
    caption = "MCMC diagnostics for the secondary chosen-category and combined models."), sep = "\n")

}
```

### Replication assessment

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
bind_rows(original |> mutate(Study = "Original: Exp1"),
          phase1_estimates |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication")) |>
  filter(pair_type == "unchosen") |>
  transmute(Study, `Pair type` = pair_type, N, OR = round(odds_ratio, 3),
            `95% HPDI` = format_hpdi(lower, upper)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Primary unchosen-category model intercept: original published OR and Phase 1 posterior median OR, with 95% HPD intervals. The chosen and combined models are secondary and do not determine the replication assessment.")
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| echo: false
if (nrow(phase1_estimates)) phase1_estimates |>
  filter(pair_type == "unchosen") |>
  transmute(`Predicted direction (OR<1)` = odds_ratio < 1,
    `95% HPDI below1` = upper < 1,
    `95% HPDI includes original0.69` = lower <= 0.69 & upper >= 0.69) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Replication checks for the primary unchosen-category estimate: predicted direction, HPDI below 1, and whether the HPDI includes the original OR.")
```


For the primary unchosen-item analysis, the effect was in the predicted direction (OR = 0.84, 95% HPDI [0.63, 1.10]), but the credible interval included 1, indicating that the evidence was inconclusive. The interval also included the original estimate (OR = 0.69), with P(OR < 1) = 0.89. For the secondary chosen-item analysis, the effect was in the predicted direction (OR = 1.46, 95% HPDI [1.11, 1.93]), with the credible interval excluding 1, supporting replication of the effect, although the estimate was smaller than the original (OR = 2.01).

### Exploratory analyses

Following the original authors’ exploratory analyses, I examined response times (RTs), memory performance, and their relationships with adaptive choice.

Unchosen pairs were not credibly associated with slower responses (RT ratio = 1.03, 95% HPDI [0.98, 1.08]). RT did not credibly predict adaptive choice (OR = 0.97, 95% HPDI [0.89, 1.05]), and there was no credible interaction between RT and pair type (OR = 1.09, 95% HPDI [0.97, 1.22]). However, choices on unchosen pairs were less adaptive (OR = 0.77, 95% HPDI [0.69, 0.86]).

For memory performance, item recognition accuracy was 0.86, associative memory accuracy was 0.78, and the corrected memory score was 0.65. The corrected memory score was not significantly correlated with adaptive choice for either chosen pairs (ρ = −0.02, p = .85) or unchosen pairs (ρ = 0.08, p = .40), and the difference between these correlations was not significant (p = .46).

```{r}
#| label: exploratory-rt
#| dependson: analysis-functions
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr list(id = experiment_id, hashes = tools::md5sum(analysis_input_files[file.exists(analysis_input_files)]), rstanarm = as.character(packageVersion("rstanarm")), coin = as.character(packageVersion("coin")))
#| results: asis
# Wang et al. (2026), sections 2.4.3–2.4.4; OSF xjhkf,
# Experiment_1_analysis.Rmd: RT models (1194–1217, 1354–1374), memory
# scoring (1690–1745, 1913–1920), corrected correlations (2141–2217).
# Agreed Phase 1 scope: RT models, descriptive memory, and memory-choice
# Spearman/permutation analyses. The recruitment-source comparison is not
# applicable to this single-source Prolific sample. Additional source-Rmd
# memory regression models remain outside the Phase 1 replication scope.
prepare_exploratory_choices <- function(d) {
  # Follow original Experiment 1: start with the same preference-filtered
  # trials as the primary choice models, then apply RT response checks.
  d$model_data |>
    filter(pair_type %in% c("chosen", "unchosen"), !timed_out,
           !is.na(p_ns), is.finite(rt), rt > 0) |>
    mutate(pid = factor(participant_id),
           trial_type = as.integer(pair_type == "unchosen"),
           adaptive = if_else(pair_type == "chosen", p_ns, 1L - p_ns)) |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    mutate(z_rt = if (n() > 1L && sd(rt) > 0) as.numeric(scale(rt)) else NA_real_) |>
    ungroup()
}
score_exploratory_memory <- function(d) {
  items <- d$retained |> filter(task == "item_memory") |>
    mutate(old = as_bool(is_old), recognized = as_bool(responded_old))
  associations <- d$retained |> filter(task == "associative_memory") |>
    select(participant_id, memory_id, response, option_roles)
  # Match by explicit memory ID, not adjacent trial indices or row order.
  stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(items[c("participant_id", "memory_id")]),
            !anyDuplicated(associations[c("participant_id", "memory_id")]))
  selected_role <- function(response, roles) {
    index <- suppressWarnings(as.integer(response))
    if (is.na(index)) return(NA_character_) # Timed-out pairing: no credit.
    options <- jsonlite::fromJSON(roles)
    stopifnot(index >= 1L, index <= length(options))
    options[[index]]
  }
  associations <- associations |>
    mutate(role = map2_chr(response, option_roles, selected_role),
           association_present = TRUE)
  scored <- items |> filter(old) |>
    left_join(associations, by = c("participant_id", "memory_id"),
              suffix = c("", "_association"))
  # A recognized cue must have its conditional pairing record. Missing export
  # records are not silently converted to errors or fabricated responses.
  stopifnot(all(!scored$recognized | !is.na(scored$association_present)))
  scored <- scored |>
    mutate(category_credit = recognized & coalesce(role %in% c("target", "same_category_lure"), FALSE),
           item_credit = recognized & coalesce(role == "target", FALSE),
           points = as.integer(recognized) + as.integer(category_credit) + as.integer(item_credit))
  old_scores <- scored |> group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(old_trials = n(), raw_memory = mean(points) / 3, .groups = "drop")
  foils <- items |> filter(!old) |> group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(foil_trials = n(), false_alarm_rate = mean(recognized), .groups = "drop")
  old_scores |> full_join(foils, by = "participant_id") |>
    mutate(corrected_memory = if_else(old_trials == 4L & foil_trials == 4L,
                                      raw_memory - false_alarm_rate, NA_real_))
}
score_associative_accuracy <- function(d) {
  # Original Experiment 1 Rmd, lines 368-378: divide correct pair responses
  # by all four old cues. As in the original grouped summary, participants
  # without any pairing records do not contribute to this descriptive mean.
  # This does not alter inclusion in the primary choice analyses.
  d$retained |> filter(task == "associative_memory") |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(pairing_trials = n(), correct_pairings = sum(as_bool(correct)),
      association_accuracy = correct_pairings / 4, .groups = "drop")
}
safe_spearman <- function(x, y) {
  if (length(x) < 2L || n_distinct(x) < 2L || n_distinct(y) < 2L) return(NA_real_)
  unname(cor(x, y, method = "spearman"))
}
spearman_permutation <- function(x, y, B = 10000L, seed = 123L) {
  valid <- is.finite(x) & is.finite(y)
  d <- tibble(corrected_memory_score = x[valid], higher_outcome_chosen = y[valid])
  observed <- safe_spearman(d$corrected_memory_score, d$higher_outcome_chosen)
  if (!is.finite(observed)) return(tibble(N = nrow(d), rho = NA_real_,
    `Permutation p (two-sided)` = NA_real_, `Valid permutations` = 0L,
    Status = "Not estimable: insufficient complete pairs or no variation"))
  set.seed(seed)
  # Original Experiment 1 Rmd, lines 2161-2180: use coin's implementation.
  # The explicit seed makes repeated report runs reproducible.
  test <- coin::spearman_test(corrected_memory_score ~ higher_outcome_chosen,
    data = d, distribution = coin::approximate(nresample = B))
  tibble(N = nrow(d), rho = observed,
    `Permutation p (two-sided)` = as.numeric(coin::pvalue(test)),
    `Valid permutations` = B, Status = "Exploratory: authors' coin::spearman_test")
}
memory_correlation_difference <- function(d, B = 10000L, seed = 123L) {
  # Original Rmd, lines 2182-2217: shuffle pooled trial-type labels over all
  # available participant-by-type rows, retaining undefined null correlations.
  pooled <- d |>
    filter(pair_type %in% c("chosen", "unchosen"),
           is.finite(corrected_memory), is.finite(adaptive_proportion)) |>
    mutate(chosen_trial_name = if_else(pair_type == "chosen", "Chosen", "Unchosen"))
  chosen <- pooled$chosen_trial_name == "Chosen"
  observed <- safe_spearman(pooled$corrected_memory[chosen], pooled$adaptive_proportion[chosen]) -
    safe_spearman(pooled$corrected_memory[!chosen], pooled$adaptive_proportion[!chosen])
  counts <- tibble(N = n_distinct(pooled$participant_id),
    `N chosen` = sum(chosen), `N unchosen` = sum(!chosen))
  if (!is.finite(observed)) return(counts |>
    mutate(`rho chosen minus unchosen` = observed, `Permutation p (two-sided)` = NA_real_,
      `Valid permutations` = 0L, Status = "Not estimable: insufficient pairs or no variation"))
  set.seed(seed)
  null_diffs <- numeric(B)
  for (i in seq_len(B)) {
    shuffled_group <- sample(pooled$chosen_trial_name)
    shuffled_chosen <- shuffled_group == "Chosen"
    rho_chosen_perm <- safe_spearman(pooled$corrected_memory[shuffled_chosen],
                                    pooled$adaptive_proportion[shuffled_chosen])
    rho_unchosen_perm <- safe_spearman(pooled$corrected_memory[!shuffled_chosen],
                                      pooled$adaptive_proportion[!shuffled_chosen])
    null_diffs[i] <- rho_chosen_perm - rho_unchosen_perm
  }
  # Match the authors' raw tail proportion exactly: no extra correction,
  # comparison tolerance, or removal of undefined shuffled correlations.
  p_value <- mean(abs(null_diffs) >= abs(observed))
  counts |>
    mutate(`rho chosen minus unchosen` = observed, `Permutation p (two-sided)` = p_value,
      `Valid permutations` = sum(is.finite(null_diffs)),
      Status = if (is.finite(p_value)) "Exploratory: authors' pooled-label shuffle" else
        "Not estimable: undefined shuffled correlations in the authors' test")
}
fit_exploratory_rt <- function(x) {
  if (n_distinct(x$pid) < 2L || n_distinct(x$trial_type) < 2L) return(list())
  # Source RT model uses default fixed-effect/intercept/auxiliary priors;
  # source RT-choice model explicitly uses normal(0, 2.5). Preserve that
  # distinction instead of borrowing logistic priors for raw RT in ms.
  rt_fit <- rstanarm::stan_glmer(rt ~ trial_type + (1 | pid), data = x,
    family = inverse.gaussian(link = "log"),
    prior_covariance = rstanarm::decov(regularization = 1),
    chains = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 123, refresh = 0)
  sampler <- rstan::get_sampler_params(rt_fit$stanfit, inc_warmup = FALSE)
  if (sum(vapply(sampler, function(s) sum(s[, "divergent__"]), numeric(1))) > 0) {
    rt_fit <- update(rt_fit, adapt_delta = 0.99, refresh = 0)
    attr(rt_fit, "tolerance_tightened") <- TRUE
  }
  fits <- list(`RT by trial type` = rt_fit)
  choice_data <- x |> filter(is.finite(z_rt))
  if (n_distinct(choice_data$pid) >= 2L && n_distinct(choice_data$trial_type) == 2L &&
      n_distinct(choice_data$adaptive) == 2L) {
    fits[["Adaptive choice by RT"]] <- fit_source_model(choice_data,
      adaptive ~ trial_type * z_rt + (1 | pid))
  }
  fits
}
exploratory_fixed_effects <- function(fits) {
  imap_dfr(fits, function(fit, model) {
    map_dfr(names(rstanarm::fixef(fit)), function(term) {
      draws <- as.matrix(fit)[, term]
      hpdi <- coda::HPDinterval(coda::mcmc(draws), prob = 0.95)[1, ]
      tibble(Model = model, Term = term, `Log coefficient` = median(draws),
        `95% HPDI lower (log)` = hpdi[1], `95% HPDI upper (log)` = hpdi[2],
        `Exponentiated coefficient` = exp(median(draws)),
        `95% HPDI lower (exp)` = exp(hpdi[1]), `95% HPDI upper (exp)` = exp(hpdi[2]))
    })
  })
}
exploratory_diagnostic_status <- function(fits) {
  diagnostics(fits) |>
    mutate(`Estimates reportable` = is.finite(`Maximum Rhat`) & `Maximum Rhat` <= 1.01 &
             is.finite(`Minimum effective N`) & `Minimum effective N` >= 400 & Divergences == 0L)
}
show_exploratory_table <- function(x, caption, digits = 3) {
  cat(knitr::kable(x, digits = digits, caption = caption), sep = "\n")
  cat("\n\n")
}
exploratory_choices <- prepare_exploratory_choices(phase1)
exploratory_memory <- score_exploratory_memory(phase1)
exploratory_rt_fits <- fit_exploratory_rt(exploratory_choices)
show_exploratory_table(
  exploratory_choices |> group_by(pair_type) |>
    summarise(N = n_distinct(participant_id), Trials = n(),
      `Mean RT (ms)` = mean(rt), `SD RT (ms)` = sd(rt), .groups = "drop"),
  "Exploratory final-choice RTs: preference-filtered choice trials with finite, positive RT; no additional RT trimming.", 1)
if (length(exploratory_rt_fits)) {
  exploratory_diagnostics <- exploratory_diagnostic_status(exploratory_rt_fits)
  reportable_models <- exploratory_diagnostics$Model[exploratory_diagnostics$`Estimates reportable`]
  withheld_models <- exploratory_diagnostics$Model[!exploratory_diagnostics$`Estimates reportable`]
  if (length(reportable_models)) show_exploratory_table(
    exploratory_fixed_effects(exploratory_rt_fits[reportable_models]),
    "Exploratory Bayesian RT models. Exponentiated RT slopes are RT ratios; the exponentiated RT intercept is baseline RT in milliseconds. Exponentiated logistic coefficients are odds ratios for adaptive choice. Trial type: chosen = 0, unchosen = 1; RT z-scores are within participant.")
  if (length(withheld_models)) cat(paste0(
    "Estimates withheld because sampler diagnostics failed: ",
    paste(withheld_models, collapse = ", "),
    ". The source model and priors are retained; no substitute model was fitted.\n\n"))
  show_exploratory_table(exploratory_diagnostics,
    paste0("MCMC diagnostics for exploratory models (N = ",
      n_distinct(exploratory_choices$participant_id),
      "). Estimates require maximum Rhat <= 1.01, minimum effective N >= 400 and zero divergences."))
  if (!"Adaptive choice by RT" %in% names(exploratory_rt_fits))
    cat("Adaptive-choice RT model not estimable: insufficient participants, trial types, RT variation, or outcome variation.\n\n")
} else {
  cat("Exploratory RT models not estimable: fewer than two participants or missing trial-type variation.\n\n")
}
memory_checks <- phase1$retained |> filter(task == "item_memory") |>
  group_by(participant_id) |> summarise(item_accuracy = mean(as_bool(correct)), .groups = "drop")
association_checks <- score_associative_accuracy(phase1)
show_exploratory_table(
  memory_checks |> left_join(association_checks, by = "participant_id") |>
    left_join(exploratory_memory, by = "participant_id") |>
    summarise(N = n(), `Mean item accuracy` = mean(item_accuracy),
      `N with associative-memory records` = sum(is.finite(association_accuracy)),
      `Mean associative accuracy` = if (any(is.finite(association_accuracy)))
        mean(association_accuracy, na.rm = TRUE) else NA_real_,
      `SD associative accuracy` = sd(association_accuracy, na.rm = TRUE),
      `N with complete corrected score` = sum(is.finite(corrected_memory)),
      `Mean corrected memory score` = mean(corrected_memory, na.rm = TRUE)),
  "Memory checks and corrected score. Per-participant associative accuracy is correct pairing responses divided by four old cues, matching the original code; its mean and SD use participants with pairing records. The separate corrected score includes all four old cues, then subtracts the false-alarm rate across four novel items.")
# Match source aggregation over preference-filtered positive-RT trials; the same
# participant memory score is related separately to chosen/unchosen choices.
memory_choice <- exploratory_choices |> group_by(participant_id, pair_type) |>
  summarise(adaptive_proportion = mean(adaptive), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(exploratory_memory, by = "participant_id")
memory_correlations <- map_dfr(c("chosen", "unchosen"), function(type) {
  d <- memory_choice |> filter(pair_type == type)
  spearman_permutation(d$corrected_memory, d$adaptive_proportion) |>
    mutate(`Pair type` = type, .before = 1)
})
show_exploratory_table(memory_correlations,
  "Exploratory corrected-memory versus adaptive-choice Spearman correlations. Authors' coin::spearman_test with 10,000 approximate resamples, two-sided p-values and seed 123; participants need a complete memory score.")
show_exploratory_table(memory_correlation_difference(memory_choice),
  "Exploratory difference in Spearman correlations (chosen minus unchosen), using the authors' pooled trial-type-label shuffle over available participant-by-type rows: 10,000 permutations, seed 123, raw two-sided permutation tail proportion. Undefined shuffled correlations leave the p-value unavailable.")
```

#### Post hoc analyses (not preregistered)

The following post hoc analyses were conducted after inspecting the data and were not preregistered. These analyses are exploratory and hypothesis-generating, and the results should be interpreted cautiously given the number of uncorrected statistical tests.

Median instruction reading times ranged from 7 to 27 seconds per page, with 5-25 participants spending less than 3 seconds on each page. Total instruction reading time was not correlated with the unchosen-item effect (ρ = -0.01).

For attention checks, 81 of 117 participants answered all questions correctly. Attention-check accuracy was not significantly correlated with the unchosen-item effect (ρ = 0.08, p = .41), but was positively correlated with the chosen-item effect (ρ = 0.24, p = .01). Most other engagement measures were not significantly related to the effects, except that longer written explanations were associated with a stronger unchosen-item effect (ρ = -0.21, p = .02).

The unchosen-item effect weakened over the course of the session (OR = 1.07 per 12 trials, 95% HPDI [1.00, 1.15], P(OR > 1) = 0.97), whereas the chosen-item effect remained relatively stable (OR = 1.01, 95% HPDI [0.94, 1.09]). Median response times also decreased from 1,606 ms in the first block of 12 trials to 1,111 ms in the last block.

Finally, reanalyzing the original data using the current analysis criteria showed that both effects remained: the unchosen-item effect (OR = 0.66, 95% HPDI [0.48, 0.89]) and the chosen-item effect (OR = 2.24, 95% HPDI [1.54, 3.14]). These findings suggest that differences in stimuli and data processing do not fully explain the weaker effect observed in the replication.

# Post hoc (decided after seeing Phase 1 data): instruction reading time, attention

spearman <- function(a, b) {
  ok <- is.finite(a) & is.finite(b)
  ct <- suppressWarnings(cor.test(a[ok], b[ok], method = "spearman", exact = FALSE))
  sprintf("rho = %.2f, p = %.3f", ct$estimate, ct$p.value)
}

## Discussion

### Summary of replication attempt

This study attempted to replicate the unchosen-item effect reported in Experiment 1 of the original study, with 117 participants compared to 123 in the original. The primary effect was in the predicted direction (OR = 0.84, 95% HPDI [0.63, 1.10]) but was smaller in magnitude than the original estimate (OR = 0.69). The credible interval included both 1 and the original estimate, indicating that the evidence for replication was inconclusive.. Therefore, the primary effect was not successfully replicated, although the results remain compatible with the original effect. The secondary chosen-item effect was replicated (OR = 1.46, 95% HPDI [1.11, 1.93]), although its magnitude was smaller than the original estimate (OR = 2.01).

### Commentary

The exploratory analyses showed no credible relationship between response time and adaptive choice, and no significant correlation between corrected memory performance and adaptive choice. The post hoc analyses suggested that the unchosen-item effect weakened over the course of the session, while the chosen-item effect remained relatively stable. This pattern may suggest that inferred value is more fragile than directly learned value, or it may reflect general fatigue or disengagement. Response times also decreased across the session, so faster responding may have contributed to the weakening of the effect. Longer written explanations were associated with a stronger unchosen-item effect, potentially suggesting a role for deeper deliberation. This finding was post hoc and should be interpreted cautiously, especially given that other engagement measures were not related to the unchosen-item effect.

Several methodological differences may have contributed to the weaker effect. Differences in stimuli and data processing seem unlikely to fully explain the results, as reanalysis of the original data using the current criteria preserved both effects. However, the replication used shorter, rewritten instructions that omitted some of the original framing around cautious decision-making and distributed deliberation instructions across practice rounds rather than presenting them all at the beginning. These changes may have affected participants' understanding of the task. Additionally, the preregistered power analysis targeted 80% power, meaning that even if the original effect were present at the assumed magnitude, there would still be approximately a 20% chance of failing to detect it. The original effect size may also have been overestimated, meaning that a larger sample might be needed to reliably detect the true effect.

There were also several challenges in reproducing the original study. Some materials, including the final-decision instructions, title cards, and written-reason prompt, were not archived, preventing an exact reproduction of the procedure. The original paper, code, and data also differed in several aspects, including the stimulus set, exclusion rule, practice response window, attention-check window, memory-test lures, use of signed versus absolute rating differences, and coding of timed-out final choices as selections of the right-side image. These discrepancies were addressed on a case-by-case basis by carefully considering the paper, code, and data and making reasonable adjustments where necessary. However, the decisions made during this process may have introduced methodological differences that influenced the results.

Overall, the replication estimate remains compatible with the original effect, a smaller effect, or no effect, making it difficult to distinguish among these possibilities. A larger follow-up study could help clarify the strength and reliability of the unchosen-item effect.

# Phase 2: Extension

**Track:** Best-practices rescue

## Rationale

Phase 1 did not successfully replicate the primary unchosen-item effect, although the effect was in the predicted direction. One possible reason is insufficient statistical power. The original power analysis targeted 80% power, leaving about a 20% chance of missing the effect even if it was present at the assumed magnitude. The original effect size may also have been overestimated, so the true effect could be smaller. Phase 2 may therefore use a larger sample to improve power and obtain a more precise estimate.

Other possible explanations include differences in task instructions, understanding, and engagement. Phase 1 used shorter, rewritten instructions and spread the deliberation instructions across practice rounds, which may have affected how participants understood the task. Phase 2 will more closely follow the original instructions and may add a comprehension check to assess understanding without revealing the hypothesis. In Phase 1, participants who failed attention checks often pressed J or K instead of the displayed letter, suggesting confusion with the choice keys. Phase 2 may add an attention-check practice and apply the original Experiment 2 attention-check exclusion rule. Additional measures of engagement may also be included. Finally, the unchosen-item effect weakened across trials, possibly due to fatigue or less stable inferred values. Phase 2 may address this by reducing the number of trials or examining the effect separately in early and late trials.

## Changes from Phase 1

Rows marked Proposed describe changes that have not yet been finalized for Phase 2.

| \# | Category | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Why |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| 1 | Sample | 117 analysed participants; 118 planned | Proposed: Recruit a larger sample if budget allows; final N TBD | Increase power and obtain a more precise estimate, especially if the true effect is smaller than originally estimated. |
| 2 | Sample | No specified Prolific approval-rate filter | Proposed: Require a Prolific approval rate of at least 95% | Better match the original study's MTurk recruitment criteria. |
| 3 | Instructions | Shortened, rewritten instructions that omitted some of the original framing | Use the original instructions with minor formatting changes and typo corrections | Restore the original framing and reduce differences in task understanding. |
| 4 | Instructions | Deliberation instructions spread across practice rounds | Present all deliberation instructions before the first practice round | Better match the original procedure. |
| 5 | Instructions | No minimum instruction reading time | Proposed: Add a minimum reading time before participants can continue; duration TBD | Encourage careful reading of the instructions. |
| 6 | Checks | No comprehension check | Proposed: Add a comprehension check. Incorrect answers return participants to the relevant instruction page for a second attempt. After a second failure: (A) show the correct answer and continue but exclude from analysis, (B) repeat until correct, or (C) end the session. Final option TBD. | Check task understanding without revealing the inferred-value relationship. |
| 7 | Checks | No attention-check practice before final choices | Proposed: Add an attention-check practice. Incorrect responses trigger a reminder to press the displayed letter rather than J or K, after which participants continue. | Reduce confusion between attention-check keys and choice-response keys. |
| 8 | Checks | Attention-check failures did not lead to exclusion | Proposed: Apply the original Experiment 2 exclusion rule: exclude participants with accuracy below 10% or nonresponses on more than 90% of attention checks. | Exclude participants showing very low attention-check performance despite practice. |
| 9 | Measurement | No tab-switch logging | Record tab switches during the task. | Provide an additional measure of participant engagement. |
| 10 | Checks | No exclusion based on tab switching | Proposed: Exclude participants based on a preregistered tab-switch criterion; threshold TBD. | Identify participants who may have disengaged from the task. |
| 11 | Trials | Original number of trials | Proposed: Option A: Reduce the number of trials. Option B: Keep the original number of trials and preregister an early-versus-late analysis of the unchosen-item effect. | Option A may reduce fatigue but would provide fewer observations for estimating individual differences and trial-level effects. Option B would allow us to test whether the effect weakens over time without changing the task or reducing the number of observations. |

Everything not listed above is identical to Phase 1.

## Power and sample

The final sample size for Phase 2 will depend on the available budget. Three approaches are being considered. The first is to target 95% power to detect the original effect using the same power analysis method as the Phase 1 preregistration, which would require 194 participants. The second is to recruit 2.5 times the original sample size (N = 308), which would provide approximately 99% power to detect the original effect. The third is a sequential design with preregistered interim analyses and stopping rules, allowing data collection in batches up to a maximum sample size determined by the budget.

A larger sample is expected to provide a more precise estimate than Phase 1, with the interval width decreasing to approximately 78% of the Phase 1 width at N = 194 and 62% at N = 308. However, if the true effect is closer to the smaller Phase 1 estimate (OR = 0.84), even 308 participants would provide only about 53% power, and approximately 600 participants would be needed to detect it reliably. The sequential approach may offer more flexibility under budget constraints. The final sample size and, if applicable, stopping rules will be decided and preregistered before data collection.

```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
# Candidate Phase 2 sample sizes named in the text (final N follows the budget):
# 194 = 95% power with the Phase 1 preregistration's method (original authors' one-sample
# t-test approximation, original Exp 1 d); 308 = 2.5 x the original N; 600 for reference.
# Model-based columns: normal approximation that scales the primary model's log-OR posterior
# SD by sqrt(N_basis / N) (Phase 1 posterior if fitted, else the original HPDI).
phase2_planned_n <- NA_integer_
phase2_candidate_n <- c(194L, 308L, 600L)
if (!is.null(phase1_fits)) {
  basis_draws <- as.matrix(phase1_fits$unchosen)[, "(Intercept)"]
  basis <- list(label = "Phase 1", n = attr(phase1_fits, "N"), sd = sd(basis_draws), or = exp(median(basis_draws)))
} else {
  basis <- list(label = "original", n = original_n, or = original$odds_ratio[original$pair_type == "unchosen"],
    sd = (log(original$upper[original$pair_type == "unchosen"]) - log(original$lower[original$pair_type == "unchosen"])) / (2 * qnorm(0.975)))
}
approx_power <- function(or, n) pnorm(abs(log(or)) / (basis$sd * sqrt(basis$n / n)) - qnorm(0.975))
tibble(N = phase2_candidate_n) |>
  mutate(`Power for original effect (t-test method)` = map_dbl(N, ~ pwr::pwr.t.test(d = original_d, n = .x,
           sig.level = 0.05, type = "one.sample", alternative = "two.sided")$power),
         `Power for original OR 0.69 (model-based)` = approx_power(0.69, N),
         `Power for Phase 1 OR (model-based)` = approx_power(basis$or, N),
         `Interval width relative to Phase 1` = sqrt(basis$n / N)) |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("Power"), ~ scales::percent(.x, accuracy = 0.1)),
         `Interval width relative to Phase 1` = round(`Interval width relative to Phase 1`, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf(paste0(
    "Candidate Phase 2 sample sizes. t-test method: the original authors' one-sample t-test approximation used for the ",
    "Phase 1 preregistration (d = %.3f). Model-based: the primary model's log-odds posterior SD (%.3f at N = %d, %s) ",
    "scaled by the square root of N; power is the probability that the 95%% interval excludes OR = 1. %s OR = %.2f."),
    original_d, basis$sd, basis$n, basis$label, basis$label, basis$or))
```

## Analysis plan

The primary analysis will follow the same approach as Phase 1, using a multilevel Bayesian logistic regression on unchosen-category trials, with the rating covariate and a participant random intercept. The model will be fitted to Phase 2 data alone, and the effect will be reported as an odds ratio (OR) with a 95% HPDI. The secondary analyses will include the chosen-category model and the combined model, as in Phase 1.

The same exclusion rules from Phase 1 will apply: sessions will end if participants miss the repeated practice choice, and incomplete sessions will be excluded. Phase 2 will also adopt the original Experiment 2 attention-check exclusion rule, excluding participants with accuracy below 10% or nonresponses on more than 90% of attention checks. Additional exclusion criteria based on comprehension-check failures or tab switching may be added.

If the original number of trials is retained, an additional analysis may test whether the unchosen-item effect changes between early and late trials by including trial position as a predictor. If a sequential sampling approach is selected, the timing of interim analyses, stopping criteria, and maximum sample size will be preregistered before data collection.

I will also report an exploratory pooled estimate combining Phase 1 and Phase 2 data. Additional exploratory analyses may examine response times and memory performance.
